:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem:
Is the function $y=f(x),$ plotted below, continuous at $x=0?$

![](images/e3/e395863ca66a7e87fa335c56e5b6aeb1ec206893e57b155bf64e5ab07be7545c.png)
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
Because there is an asymptote at $x=0,$ it is impossible to draw the function in the neighborhood of $x=0$ without taking our pencil off of the paper.

Therefore, the function $y=f(x)$ is not continuous at $x=0.$

:topic/knowledge-points.:knowledge-point/title: Determining Whether a Function Is Continuous at a Given Point

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem:
What are the points of discontinuity of the function $y=g(x),$ plotted below?

![](images/6d/6d0d3c2cd072841546e66d70105436200e316e156901f8fe27dc150e96ff3da4.png)
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution: The points of discontinuity are at $x=0,$ $x=1,$ and $x=2.5.$ It is impossible to draw the function in the neighborhood of these three points without taking our pencil off of the page.

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem:
![](images/18/1867a80955ae4b456cbcb011eefed96431f2b12926994942613eb947e55e38c6.png)

 

The graph of $y=f(x)$ is shown above. Which of the following statements are true? 

- $f(x)$ is defined at $x=2$

- $\lim_\limits{x\rightarrow \, 2}f(x)$ exists

- $f(x)$ is continuous at $x=2$
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
By inspecting the graph, we can conclude the following:

- Statement I is true. Indeed, $f(2)=2.$

- Statement II is false. From the graph, we can see that the left and right-sided limits are different:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \,{2}^{-}}f(x) & =2, \\ {lim}_{x\to \,{2}^{+}}f(x) & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,  $\lim_\limits{x\rightarrow \, 2}f(x)$ does not exist.

- Statement III is false.  The graph of the function breaks at $x=2.$ It's impossible to draw the graph of $f(x)$ without taking our pencil off of the paper. Therefore, $f(x)$ is not continuous at $x=2.$

In conclusion, only statement I is true.
